183.title: At-Tin: the fig and the olive
183.hook: by the fig, the olive, Sinai and the safe city, the human was made in the best stature (Surah 95)
183.howItsDone: At-Tin is recited in the prayers, and the Prophet recited it in the evening prayer while traveling; its verse on the best stature is often quoted in teaching about human dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Alaq, and the man who tried to stop a servant from praying. Your line was bow and draw near. Did you go low, on purpose, and what was it like? Day one hundred eighty-three.

A companion of the Prophet named al-Bara' remembered one night on a journey. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ led the evening prayer and recited a short surah that starts with fruit: by the fig and the olive. Al-Bara' said, and it's recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, that he had never heard anyone with a more beautiful voice or recitation. Of all the things he might have remembered from his time with the Prophet, he remembered a voice, at night, reciting about figs. Today: At-Tin, the fig and the olive.
screen: `A NIGHT ON A JOURNEY.` → `BY THE FIG AND THE OLIVE.` → `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL VOICE.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-five opens with four oaths, in Pickthall's translation: By the fig and the olive, By Mount Sinai, And by this land made safe. Why fig and olive? Commentators give two answers, and hold both. The fruits themselves, gifts of the earth, sweet and nourishing. And the places they grow: some commentators link the fig and olive to the lands around Jerusalem, home to earlier prophets. Mount Sinai is where Musa received revelation. And this land made safe is Mecca, where the Prophet was. So some scholars read the oaths as a map of revelation: the lands of the prophets, Musa's mountain, Muhammad's city. Then the point of all four oaths: Surely We created man of the best stature. Ahsan taqwim, the finest form, the best proportion, body and mind and soul. That's the Qur'an's starting point about human beings: made well, beautifully, on purpose. Then the surah adds a hard line: then We reduced him to the lowest of the low. Commentators read it several ways: old age and frailty, or the fall that comes when a person turns away. Except, it says, those who believe and do good. They have a reward that never ends. So the surah holds both. You were made in the best form, and you can fall far from it. The dignity is the beginning, not something you have to earn. What you do with it is the story. Made in the best form.
screen: `FIG, OLIVE, SINAI, THE SAFE LAND.` · `A MAP OF REVELATION.` · `AHSAN TAQWIM — THE BEST STATURE.` · `THE LOWEST OF THE LOW, EXCEPT —` · then, large: `MADE IN THE BEST FORM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you have a fig or an olive, or any fruit, hold it now. Look at it closely. The color, the skin, how it's put together. Then eat it slowly, and if you pray, you can say bismillah first and alhamdulillah after. If you don't have one, look at your own hand the same way: the joints, the lines, how it moves. Made in the best form. The bell holds the time.
At-Tin. The fig, the first oath of Surah ninety-five, which says the human was made in the best stature. Today's word.
Your line: made in the best form. When you catch yourself in a mirror today, or put someone else down in your head, remember: the dignity comes first. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: Ash-Sharh: the opened chest
184.hook: did We not expand your chest and lift your burden (94:1–3)
184.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Musa's supplication from Surah Ta-Ha, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before exams, speeches and difficult tasks, and Surah ash-Sharh is often recited in times of stress.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Tin, the fig and the olive, and the human made in the best stature. Your line was made in the best form. Did you catch yourself remembering that dignity comes first? Day one hundred eighty-four.

Stress has an address, and often it's the chest. It gets tight. Breathing gets shallow. My chest is heavy, people say. I've got a weight on me. And when it lifts, when the news is good, when the fight is over, the first thing people do is take a long, full breath. Today's surah is about exactly that feeling. It's spoken to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in hard years in Mecca, and it starts with a question about his chest. Today: Ash-Sharh, the opened chest.
screen: `STRESS LIVES IN THE CHEST.` → `A WEIGHT ON ME.` → `THEN, A LONG BREATH.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate, And eased thee of the burden Which weighed down thy back. Sharh means opening, expanding, making wide. In Arabic, a narrow chest is anxiety, grief, feeling trapped. An opened chest is relief, calm, room to breathe, and also room to understand, to accept. The surah asks, as if reminding a friend: didn't We open your chest? Didn't We take off the weight that was breaking your back? It's a reassurance spoken in the past tense: look, it already happened. Commentators give the opening two senses. One is inward: the calm, the guidance and the strength to carry the revelation. The other, some connect with a report in Sahih Muslim: when the Prophet was a young boy, playing with other children, Jibril came, opened his chest, washed his heart with Zamzam water, and closed it again. The surah then adds: and We raised your name, your remembrance. Commentators point to the call to prayer, where his name is said after Allah's. There's another opened chest in the Qur'an. Musa, sent to face Pharaoh, prays: my Lord, expand my chest for me, and ease my task. You'll hear his words, rabbi ishrah li sadri, before an exam, a hard talk, a speech. So the chest that's heavy isn't the end of the story. The Qur'an treats it as something that can be opened, and a burden as something that can be lifted. The burden lifts.
screen: `SHARH — OPENING, MAKING WIDE.` · `THE BURDEN THAT WEIGHED DOWN THY BACK.` · `WE RAISED YOUR NAME.` · `RABBI ISHRAH LI SADRI.` · then, large: `THE BURDEN LIFTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe deeply into your chest. Sit up, and put one hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly, and feel it rise and widen under your hand. Breathe out, and let the shoulders drop. Again. Let each in-breath make a little more room. If something heavy is sitting there, name it, and let the next out-breath carry some of it away. If you pray, you can say Musa's words: rabbi ishrah li sadri. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Sharh. The opening, the widening of the chest; the name of Surah ninety-four. Today's word.
Your line: the burden lifts. When your chest gets tight today, stop and take three wide breaths, hand on your chest. Remember one weight that has already lifted. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: Ash-Sharh: with hardship, ease
185.hook: with hardship comes ease, said twice (94:5–6)
185.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 94:5–6, inna ma'a al-'usri yusra, to comfort each other in illness, loss and hard times, and the verse is common in calligraphy in homes and on cards.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh, the opened chest. Your line was the burden lifts. When your chest got tight, did you stop for three wide breaths? Day one hundred eighty-five.

Some sentences get written on hospital whiteboards, taped above desks during exam season, texted at three in the morning to a friend whose marriage just ended. One short Qur'anic line turns up in places like these: in Arabic calligraphy on living-room walls, on phone lock screens, on the last page of a student's notebook. It's said twice in a row, and the way it's worded is more hopeful than a quick reading suggests. Today: Ash-Sharh again, with hardship, ease.
screen: `ON WHITEBOARDS, DESKS, LOCK SCREENS.` → `SAID TWICE IN A ROW.` → `MORE HOPEFUL THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the opened chest, the lifted burden, the raised name. Then the surah says, in Pickthall's translation: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice the first small word: ma'a, with. Not after hardship. With it. The ease isn't only waiting at the end of the hard thing; it's already inside it, traveling alongside. Even a hard stretch often has something in it that holds a person up: a friend who shows up, a night of good sleep, a moment of laughter at the hospital. Now notice the grammar, which classical commentators dwelt on. In Arabic, hardship is al-'usr, with the word the: the hardship, the same one both times. But ease is yusr, without the: an ease, and then another ease. So the same hardship, said twice, meets two different eases. A saying reported from early Muslims puts it this way: one hardship will never overcome two eases. Scholars discuss how firmly that saying traces back, but commentators still teach the reading of the grammar. Then the surah ends with what to do: when you're free of one task, keep working, and turn to your Lord with longing. Not sit and wait for ease. Keep going, toward Him. Tradition places this surah in the hard years in Mecca, when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had few followers and the pressure was heavy. It didn't promise that the hardship would vanish. It promised company for it. With hardship, ease.
screen: `MA'A — WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `THE HARDSHIP, AND AN EASE.` · `ONE HARDSHIP, TWO EASES.` · `WHEN FREE, KEEP WORKING, TOWARD HIM.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the ease inside a hard thing. Sit, and bring one hard thing to mind, something you're in the middle of right now. Don't try to fix it. Just look at it honestly. Then look for what's traveling alongside it. A person who's helped. Something you've learned. A small good that came only because of this. Name one ease. Then look again, and see if there's a second. The bell holds the time.
Ash-Sharh. The opened chest, and the surah that says twice: with hardship comes ease. Today's word.
Your line: with hardship, ease. Send the line to one person going through something hard today. Or keep it for yourself, and look for the ease that's already there. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: Ad-Duha: the morning
186.hook: your Lord has not left you, and what comes after is better (93:1–5)
186.tomorrow: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker
186.howItsDone: Many Muslims turn to Surah ad-Duha in times of sadness or waiting; the mid-morning voluntary prayer, salat ad-duha, shares its name with the surah's first word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ash-Sharh again, and the line said twice. Your line was with hardship, ease. Did you find the ease traveling inside a hard thing, maybe even two? Day one hundred eighty-six.

You text someone you love, and they don't answer. An hour. A day. A week. And your mind fills the silence: they're angry, they're done with me, I did something wrong. Silence is where the worst stories get written. Something like that happened to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In the early years of revelation, the verses stopped coming. Days passed, then more. And people around him noticed, and some of them were cruel about it. The silence ended with this surah, and its first word is light. Today: Ad-Duha, the morning.
screen: `THE TEXT THAT ISN'T ANSWERED.` → `SILENCE WRITES THE WORST STORIES.` → `THE REVELATION PAUSED.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records that the Prophet fell ill and didn't rise for prayer at night for a few nights, and a woman taunted him that his companion, meaning the one who brought the revelation, had abandoned him. Reports differ on the length of the pause and on who said what. What they share is the silence, and the sting. Then came Surah ninety-three. In Pickthall's translation: By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee, And verily the latter portion will be better for thee than the former, And verily thy Lord will give unto thee so that thou wilt be content. Duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is warm. Look at the two oaths: the bright morning and the still night. In the surah, both belong to the same Lord. The night didn't mean the morning was gone; it was just night. Then the direct answer to the fear: your Lord has not left you, and He is not angry with you. Two sentences, answering exactly the two worst stories silence tells. Then a promise: the later will be better for you than the earlier. Commentators read it two ways: the rest of his life would be better than its beginning; and the next life better than this one. And a last line: your Lord will give you until you are content. Notice the tone. Not a lecture. Something closer to a hand on the shoulder. The later is better.
screen: `THE SILENCE, AND THE TAUNT.` · `BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.` · `NOT FORSAKEN, NOT HATED.` · `THE LATTER BETTER THAN THE FORMER.` · then, large: `THE LATER IS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one hope for later. Sit, and think of a silence in your life right now: something you're waiting on, an answer that hasn't come. Notice the story your mind is writing into it. Then set that story down. Picture the morning after a long night, the light getting warm. After the bell, write one sentence, a hope for later, that begins: later, I hope. Keep it somewhere you'll find it. The bell holds the time.
Ad-Duha. The bright morning, the name of Surah ninety-three, which says: your Lord has not left you, and the later is better. Today's word.
Your line: the later is better. When a silence starts writing a bad story in your head today, stop it mid-sentence. Remember: night isn't the absence of morning. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker
187.hook: did He not find you an orphan and shelter you, so don't be harsh with orphans or turn askers away (93:6–10)
187.howItsDone: Care for orphans holds a special place in Muslim practice, from sponsoring orphans to supporting orphanages, and many Muslims recall 93:9–10 when someone asks them for help or a question.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ad-Duha, the morning after the silence. Your line was the later is better. Did you stop a bad story mid-sentence, and write one hope for later? Day one hundred eighty-seven.

Ask someone who grew up without much why they notice certain people, and the answer is often short: I remember what it was like. The one who went to school hungry notices the kid with no lunch. The one who was new in the country notices the family that doesn't speak the language yet. Memory turns into attention. Yesterday, Surah ad-Duha reassured the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: your Lord hasn't left you. Today, the second half of the surah. It asks him to remember where he came from, and then tells him what to do with the memory. Today: Ad-Duha, the orphan and the asker.
screen: `I REMEMBER WHAT IT WAS LIKE.` → `MEMORY TURNS INTO ATTENTION.` → `WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The surah asks three questions, in Pickthall's translation: Did He not find thee an orphan and protect thee? Did He not find thee wandering and direct thee? Did He not find thee destitute and enrich thee? The early biographies fill in each line. His father died before he was born. His mother, they say, died when he was about six, and his grandfather, who took him in, two years later. Then his uncle Abu Talib raised him. An orphan three times over, and each time, someone sheltered him. Wandering, commentators say, means searching, not yet guided, before revelation came. Destitute: he was poor, and commentators often connect his later means to his marriage to Khadijah and his work in trade. Then the surah turns those three memories into two instructions: Therefor the orphan oppress not, Therefor the beggar drive not away. The Arabic for the beggar is as-sa'il, the one who asks. Some commentators read it as covering both: the one who asks for money or food, and the one who asks a question, who comes to learn. Don't brush off either one. Don't sigh at them. Don't make them feel small for asking. The Prophet said, in a hadith in Bukhari, holding up two fingers side by side: I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. The logic of the surah is simple. You were sheltered, so shelter. You were guided, so answer the one who asks. The memory of need is meant to become kindness to the needy. Don't turn the asker away.
screen: `AN ORPHAN, AND SHELTERED.` · `WANDERING, AND GUIDED.` · `AS-SA'IL — THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `LIKE THESE TWO FINGERS.` · then, large: `DON'T TURN THE ASKER AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and remember one time you needed something and someone gave it: a meal, a ride, an answer, a place to stay. Picture their face. Let the memory of being helped come back. Then decide: the next person who asks you for something today, money, time, a question, directions, gets a yes if you can, and a kind answer if you can't. No sigh. The bell holds the time.
Ad-Duha. The bright morning, and the surah that says: you were an orphan and were sheltered, so don't turn the asker away. Today's word.

Your line: don't turn the asker away. When the next person asks you for something, say yes if you can, answer kindly if you can't, and don't make them feel small for asking. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 187 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AD-DUHA: SPEAK OF THE BLESSINGS.`

188.title: Ad-Duha: speak of the blessings
188.hook: and as for the favor of your Lord, speak of it (93:11)
188.howItsDone: Many Muslims make a habit of naming blessings aloud, answering how are you with alhamdulillah and thanking the people through whom good came, while taking care that speaking of a gift doesn't become boasting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ad-Duha again, the orphan and the one who asks. Your line was don't turn the asker away. Did someone ask you for something, and did you stay long enough to hear them? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

How's it going? The answer tends to come in one of two settings. Complain, because complaining is safe and everyone can join in. Or say fine, and move on, because saying something went well feels like bragging, or like tempting fate. So the good things in a life often go unsaid. The job that worked out, the friend who showed up, the morning the pain was a little less. Ad-Duha, the surah of the morning light, ends on a line that pushes against that habit. After reminding the Prophet of everything he was given, the last word isn't keep quiet. It's the opposite. Today: the last line of Ad-Duha.
screen: `COMPLAIN, OR SAY FINE.` → `THE GOOD THINGS GO UNSAID.` → `THE LAST LINE OF AD-DUHA.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-three has eleven verses. The last three are a set of three instructions. The orphan: don't be harsh with him. The one who asks: don't drive him away. And then verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse. The Arabic is short: fa-haddith. Speak of it. Tell it. The same root gives the word hadith, a report, a thing told. So the surah that began with the morning light, and the promise that the later would be better, ends by asking for the good to be told out loud. Commentators read the bounty in more than one way. Some say it means the revelation itself: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was being told to share the revelation he had been given. Others read it more widely: every favor, from guidance to food to health, is something to acknowledge rather than hide. Some hold both at once. Scholars are careful to separate this from showing off. Speaking of a gift as a gift points past yourself to where it came from. Boasting points back at you. The difference is often just one word: I did this, or this was given to me. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi adds a human side: whoever does not thank people has not thanked God. So speaking of the bounty isn't only upward. It's also telling the teacher, the parent, the stranger at the bus stop, that what they gave you landed. The orphan, the asker, the blessing. Three verses, one direction: open hands and an open mouth.

segments.voice: Sit, and let two minutes of quiet settle. Bring to mind one good thing from this week, something given, not something you earned. Hold it long enough to see it clearly. Then think of one person you could tell about it, today, in a sentence: this happened, and I'm grateful. If you pray, you can add alhamdulillah. The bell holds the time.
Ad-Duha. The morning light, Surah ninety-three, which closes with speak of the bounty of your Lord. Today's word.
Your line: speak of the gift. Tell one person, today, one good thing that was given to you, and say thank you to someone who had a hand in it. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

189.title: Al-Layl: the night
189.hook: by the night and the day, your strivings are different (Surah 92)
189.howItsDone: Al-Layl is one of the short surahs often learned by heart and recited in the prayer; its opening oaths, by the night and the day, are often read as a reminder that every person's effort is heading somewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last line of Ad-Duha. Your line was speak of the gift. Did you tell anyone one good thing that was given to you? Day one hundred eighty-nine.

Eleven at night, one quiet street, two people under the same streetlight. One is driving home from a double shift so her kids can eat. The other is out to do something he hopes nobody finds out about. From a satellite, they look identical: two dots moving in the dark. The night covers them both. What's different is where each one is going, and why. The surah just before Ad-Duha in the Qur'an opens on that same picture. Night and day, male and female, and then a sentence that could be written about any street, any office, any family group chat. Today: Al-Layl, the night.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, THE SAME DARK STREET.` → `THE NIGHT COVERS THEM BOTH.` → `AL-LAYL, THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-two begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the night enshrouding. The night that covers, that wraps things so you can't see them. Then by the day when it shines, and by the One who created the male and the female. Three oaths, and all of them are pairs: dark and light, one and the other. Then the point the oaths were leading to. Verse four, in Pickthall's words: Lo! your effort is dispersed. Scattered, going in different directions. The Arabic word for effort is sa'y. It's effort with your feet in it, the sense of hurrying toward something. Pilgrims use the same word, sa'y, for the walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa during Hajj, retracing Hajar's run for water. And the word describing the effort, shatta, means scattered, spread apart, as different from each other as night from day. So the surah says: you are all under the same sky, but your efforts are not the same. Some run toward what's good. Some run away from it. The night hides the difference for a while. It doesn't erase it. Notice what the surah does not do. It doesn't say everyone's effort is wasted, or that effort is bad. It says effort has a direction. The next verses, which we'll open tomorrow, describe the two directions. Today is only the question. It's the end of a week, too. We began it with At-Tin, made in the best form, then Ash-Sharh, the chest opened and hardship paired with ease, then Ad-Duha, the morning, the orphan and the gift told out loud. Now the night, and the question under all of them: where is the effort going?
screen: `THREE OATHS, ALL IN PAIRS.` · `SA'Y — STRIVING, EFFORT WITH FEET.` · `SHATTA — SCATTERED, NOT THE SAME.` · `EFFORT HAS A DIRECTION.` · then, large: `EFFORTS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and for two minutes, look back over yesterday as if from above, like that satellite. Where did your effort actually go? Not where you meant it to go. Where it went. The phone, the work, a person, a worry. Don't judge it. Just notice the direction, the way you'd notice which way a river runs. The bell holds the time.
Al-Layl. The night, the name of Surah ninety-two, which swears by the night and the day and says your efforts differ. Today's word.
Your line: efforts differ. Once today, when you're about to spend real effort on something, ask which way it's pointed. Then keep going, or turn. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

match.prompt: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
pairs: the walk called sa'y in Hajj

myth: Surah 92 says all human effort is wasted
it says efforts differ: they go in different directions, not that they're pointless.
the opening oaths of Al-Layl come in pairs
night and day, male and female: opposites, before the line about differing efforts.
the walk between Safa and Marwa is also called sa'y
the same word as the effort in 92:4: hurrying, striving toward something.

fork.setup: Al-Layl swears by the night, the day, and the creation of male and female. what does it say next?
options: that night is better than day
that your efforts are diverse
that the world will end at night
fork.reveal: your striving is scattered, going in different directions. the oaths in pairs set up the point: same sky, different directions.

original.note: Arabic: the night, the name of Surah 92, which opens by swearing by the night as it covers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about nighttime.
what it means: by night and day, male and female: your efforts differ, going in different directions.

what a scholar hears: sa'yakum la-shatta. sa'y is the word for the pilgrims' walk between Safa and Marwa; shatta means dispersed, the plural of shatit. the oaths in pairs mirror the two paths the surah goes on to describe.
